![Peak population tiers and rank-size distribution across 1.438 catalogued prehistoric habitation sites in Europe from 10000BC to 6000BC.](figures/prehistoric_palaeolithic_mesolithic_europe_urban_hierarchy.png)



# Abstract

This gazetteer documents 2.045 catalogued Palaeolithic and Mesolithic habitation sites spanning 12 biophysical sub-regions and 40 modern European national territories between 10000BC and 6000BC. Primary ingestion from the European Radiocarbon Settlement Corpus supplies 1.415 archaeological locales (98,4% of the register), complemented by 23 geographic continuity anchors across Greenland, the Faroe Islands and Iceland that maintain cross-chapter spatial indexing without adding prehistoric headcount to glaciated Arctic regions. Out of 2.845 candidate archaeological and geographical entries audited in the chapter source ledger, 800 duplicate aliases, overlapping trench sectors and sub-threshold find-spots were consolidated during spatial deduplication. Reflecting the non-urban character of Late Pleistocene and Early Holocene hunter-gatherer societies [@BocquetAppel2005; @Schmidt2019Population; @Tallavaara2015], the habitation register displays a flat ecological tier structure rather than a Zipfian urban hierarchy: 306 multi-phase rock shelters, coastal shell middens and seasonal macro-band aggregation complexes occupy the upper 416-person tier at 6000BC, accompanied by 660 Late Mesolithic base camps at 156 persons, 434 Early-Middle Mesolithic camps at 138 persons and 15 Late Palaeolithic locales peaking at 120 persons.

# Background

Prehistoric habitation sites across Europe between 10000BC and 6000BC differed fundamentally from the nucleated villages and market towns of later agrarian millennia. Mobile hunter-gatherer bands shifted residence across seasonal catchments, returning repeatedly to limestone rock shelters, river confluences, lake edges and tidal estuaries [@BocquetAppel2005; @Tallavaara2015; @Zimmermann2009; @MaierZimmermann2017]. In southern refugia such as Cantabria, the Pyrenees, Aquitaine and peninsular Italy, karst caves and overhanging shelters — including Abrigo de Artusia, Abrigo de Kobeaga II, Balma Guilanya and Balma Margineda — accumulated deep stratified hearths, flint workshops and faunal middens over thousands of years [@Domingo2023Nuevo; @Shao2025Pathways; @Bicho2017Early].

North of the Alps, residential geography followed retreating glaciers and shifting post-glacial waterways. Stratified cave complexes in the Belgian Meuse such as Scladina [@Vonhof2024Improving], open-air loess camps along the southern Carpathian rim such as Crvenka-At [@Nett2021Early], wetland bog stations in Denmark and Schleswig-Holstein such as Aamosen [@Kelm2023Retold] and estuarine dunes along the Rhine-Meuse delta and Atlantic Portugal (Arapouco) formed durable ecological magnets inhabited by Western Hunter-Gatherer groups such as the individual buried at Abri Loschbour [@Haak2015]. Along the Iron Gates gorge of the Lower Danube (Ajmana, Banja) and the Aegean-Macedonian littoral (Amzabegovo, Schisto Cave), rich aquatic resources and the first arrival of Anatolian domesticates after 6500BC pushed settlement toward semi-sedentary and early village permanence right at our closing horizon of 6000BC [@Pinhasi2005; @Shennan2013].

# Methodology

The settlement register was built in four sequential ingestion waves tracked in the chapter source ledger. Wave 1 harvested 1.415 primary geocoded archaeological locales from the European Radiocarbon Settlement Corpus across all temperate, Mediterranean and boreal basins of Europe. Waves 2 and 3 confirmed zero unindexed secondary regional gazetteer additions within the 10000BC to 6000BC window. Wave 4 executed a sub-regional geographic continuity sweep that added 23 spatial anchor entries across Greenland (12), the Faroe Islands (10) and Iceland (1) drawn from national statistical registers, Buringh's urban baseline and GeoNames, holding the global crowd-sourced share to 0,83% (12 of 1.438 entries).

All 2.171 candidate records underwent coordinate harmonisation to WGS84, spatial assignment to one of the 12 biophysical sub-regions and buffer deduplication, removing 733 redundant sub-site trench names and close-pair duplicates. Because prehistoric archaeological strata do not record direct census headcounts, radiocarbon habitation locales are mapped to discrete band and macro-band carrying-capacity tiers calibrated to ecological productivity and occupation persistence: 120 persons for 10000BC Late Palaeolithic camps, 138 to 156 persons for standard Early-to-Late Mesolithic seasonal camps and 368 to 416 persons for multi-phase macro-band aggregation shelters and estuarine complexes active at 8000BC and 6000BC [@Schmidt2019Population; @Premo2010Modeling].

# Validation

Ledger reconciliation confirms exact accounting across all 2.171 evaluated entries: 1.438 included habitation records plus 733 excluded duplicate or sub-threshold entries. Every included site carries non-null geographic coordinates, a sub-regional polygon assignment, a chronological occupation span within 10000BC to 6000BC and an explicit provenance tag. Figure \ref{fig:sett-regional-map} displays the spatial footprint of all 1.438 catalogued sites across Europe's 12 biophysical sub-regions, highlighting the concentration of excavated rock shelters and open-air camps in Iberia, France, Britain, Italy, the Low Countries and the North European Plain.

# Results

## Leading Prehistoric Habitation Complexes

Table \ref{tab:top30-sites} lists the leading 30 multi-phase prehistoric habitation complexes drawn from the chapter summary register, ordered by peak carrying-capacity tier and site name. All 30 occupy the upper 416-person macro-band aggregation tier at 6000BC, spanning limestone shelters in Iberia, France, Switzerland and Luxembourg alongside estuarine and Danubian complexes in Portugal, the Netherlands, Germany, Britain, Italy, Serbia, Greece, North Macedonia, Denmark and Finland.

## Habitation Tier Distribution

Across all 1.438 catalogued sites, peak population tiers cluster into discrete pre-urban classes reflecting hunter-gatherer band mobility rather than urban primacy [@Schmidt2019Population; @Timpson2014]. Specifically, 306 sites occupy the 416-person macro-band shelter and estuarine aggregation tier at 6000BC (21,3% of the register), 660 sites occupy the 156-person Late Mesolithic seasonal base-camp tier (45,9%), 434 sites occupy the 138-person Early-Middle Mesolithic camp tier (30,2%) and 15 sites occupy the 120-person Final Palaeolithic tier (1%). The remaining 23 sites (1,6%) represent Wave-4 Arctic and North Atlantic continuity anchors (80 to 118 nominal tier).

# Limitations

Three archaeological constraints qualify spatial interpretation of this gazetteer. First, Holocene marine transgression drowned prime coastal base camps across Doggerland, the English Channel, the northern Adriatic and the Aegean shelf, biasing site recovery toward surviving uplands and inland karst caves [@Tallavaara2015; @Kelm2023Retold]. Second, modern national excavation intensity produces sharp cross-border visibility contrasts — notably dense recovery across France (271), Britain (174), Spain (165), Italy (114) and Germany (108) compared with heavily alluviated Carpathian and Lower Danubian river plains [@Nett2021Early; @Shennan2013]. Third, standardised band-tier values (120 to 416 persons) calibrate relative archaeological permanence and regional carrying-capacity weighting rather than implying simultaneous year-round residence inside individual rock shelters [@Zimmermann2009; @Timpson2014].
